rows.title: Open problem: Fourier entropy versus total influence
rows.body:
OPEN PROBLEM from the Codex campaign ledger (source_says_open; current status unverified; result status attempted_unsolved). Bound the Shannon entropy of the squared Fourier coefficients of every Boolean function by a universal constant times its total influence. Source: O Donnell: Open problems in analysis of Boolean functions, PDF p.5, Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture.
Posed in O Donnell: Open problems in analysis of Boolean functions
Status as recorded in the campaign ledger on 2026-09-07

rows.title: Attempt on Fourier entropy versus total influence
rows.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Fourier entropy versus total influence exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: Discarding the Boolean constraint destroys the claim: the probability measure uniform on the n singleton subsets has entropy log2(n) but mean subset size1. It cannot be the squared spectrum of a Boolean function when n>=2. Check: If all Fourier mass were on singletons, f=sum_i a_i*x_i with a_i=plus/minus1/sqrt(n). In f^2 the coefficient of x_i*x_j is2*a_i*a_j, nonzero for distinct i,j, whereas Boolean f requires f^2=1. This independently exhibits the violated Fourier convolution identity. Obstruction: Entropy versus mean cardinality alone is insufficient. Any proof must use the nonlinear identities imposed by f^2=1; no dimension-free inequality exploiting all of them is obtained.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0162-fourier-entropy-versus-total-influence
No independent review

rows.title: Every read-once formula f over AND, OR and NOT satisfies H(f) <= 6.4573 I(f), where H is the Shannon entropy of the squared Fourier coeffici
rows.body: Every read-once formula f over AND, OR and NOT satisfies H(f) <= 6.4573 I(f), where H is the Shannon entropy of the squared Fourier coefficients and I the total influence. Computer-assisted: an explicit potential Gamma_hat = (value-iteration interpolant) + c p(1-p) with c = 0.01 is verified on all of (0,1)^2 by interval arithmetic (three adaptive cell regions plus analytic tails), cross-checked at 40 digits. The previously known bound for read-once formulas was 10; Hod's lower bound is 6.4548, so the constant is within 0.0025 of best possible.

rows.title: Fourier entropy-influence for linear threshold functions: H(f) <= 14.22 I(f) for every f = sgn(w.x - theta)
rows.body: Every linear threshold function f = sgn(w.x - theta) on {-1,1}^n satisfies H(f) <= 14.22 I(f), where H is the Fourier entropy and I the total influence; the class was listed as open by Chakraborty et al. (LATIN 2018, arXiv:1903.11635). Ranking coordinates by |w_i|, the derivative D_i f is the indicator of a slab of width 2|w_i|, and the Erdos-Littlewood-Offord inequality applied to noise on the heavier coordinates gives E_S sum_{i in S} ln+(r(i)/|S|) <= 4.151 I, so the spectral sample lives on the top O(|S|) coordinates by weight; entropy against a rank-weighted reference measure, plus O'Donnell-Wright-Zhou's level-entropy bound (at most 3I), gives the constant (optimum exponent a = 1.2006, 14.2142). For f = G(w.x) with G changing sign t times, H(f) <= C_t I(f) with C_t = O(log t) (16.57 at t = 2). The supremum of H/I over threshold functions appears numerically to be about 4. The rank criterion is sufficient, not necessary: it fails for recursive ternary majority.

rows.title: Fourier entropy-influence for read-k DNFs and CNFs (O(log k)), for regular functions, and for read-once formulas of threshold gates
rows.body: Every read-k DNF or CNF f (negations and redundant terms allowed) satisfies H(f) <= min(2.89 + 9.9k, 30 + 5.6 log2 k) I(f), so the Fourier entropy-influence constant grows as O(log k); before this only the min-entropy version was known for read-k DNFs (Arunachalam-Chakraborty-Koucky-Saurabh-de Wolf, STACS 2020). Every regular (2-monotone) Boolean function, including every linear threshold function, satisfies H(f) <= 15.1 I(f). Both classes satisfy O'Donnell-Tan's strengthened form H^+ <= C (I - Var). Threshold gates T_{t,r} = 1[y_1 + ... + y_r >= t] satisfy the biased strengthened form under every product measure (constant 526 in nats, about 760 bits; 66.4 bits when all inputs share one bias), so by O'Donnell-Tan's composition theorem every read-once formula of threshold gates of any fan-in and depth satisfies FEI. Monotone functions whose desirability preorder has width w satisfy H <= (15.1 + log2 w) I.

rows.title: Fourier entropy-influence: reduction to small-influence functions, a 7.05 floor for restriction inductions, and read-once formulas over AND, OR, XOR, NOT
rows.body: The Fourier entropy-influence conjecture is equivalent to its restriction to Boolean functions all of whose influences are below any fixed tau: a coordinate of influence at least tau has restriction drop Delta_i <= (2/ln 2 + log2(e/tau)) Inf_i, so a violation localizes to a subcube on which every influence is small and the restriction step fails at every coordinate. On self-compositions of Numaro's record function the restriction-step constant rho_0 = min_i Delta_i/Inf_i is 6.3290, 6.8901 and 7.0519 at 324, 5832 and 104976 variables (limit about 7.1116), so no potential-free coordinate induction can give a constant below 7.05. The XOR gate inequality is certified, so read-once formulas over AND, OR, XOR and NOT satisfy H <= 6.4573 I; a prime monotone 7-input gate breaks the read-once potential behind that bound; the five prime 3-input classes (one-hot, MAJ3, EQ3, MUX, Q3) are proved, while fan-in 3 at 6.4573 in general is numerical only. Per-coordinate erasure bounds fail even for monotone functions (majority with one flipped point gives ratio at least (n - 3 log2 n)/2). The full conjecture remains open.

rows.title: Dudley's Entropy Integral Bound (Chaining)
rows.body:
Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a sub-Gaussian process on a metric space (T, d) with sub-Gaussian increments: E[exp(lambda * (X_s - X_t))] <= exp(lambda^2 * d(s, t)^2 / 2) for all s, t in T, lambda in R. Let diam(T) = sup_{s, t in T} d(s, t). Then for an absolute constant C > 0, E[ sup_{s, t in T} (X_s - X_t) ] <= C * int_0^{diam(T)} sqrt(log N(T, d, epsilon)) d epsilon.
(X_t)_{t in T} has sub-Gaussian increments with respect to d
diam(T) < infinity

rows.title: Chain rule for Shannon entropy: H(X, Y) = H(X) + sum_x p_X(x) H(Y | X = x), and the conditional laws chosen at values x of probability zero do not matter
rows.body:
Let X and Y take finitely many values with joint pmf p and marginal p_X, entropies in natural logarithms with 0 ln 0 = 0. For each x choose a pmf K_x on the values of Y with K_x(y) = p(x, y)/p_X(x) whenever p_X(x) > 0, and K_x arbitrary when p_X(x) = 0. Then H(X, Y) = H(X) + sum over x of p_X(x) H(K_x), and this sum, the conditional entropy H(Y | X), equals -sum over (x, y) with p(x, y) > 0 of p(x, y) ln(p(x, y)/p_X(x)) whatever the choices at zero-probability x. Hence H(Y | X) >= 0 and H(X, Y) >= H(X). By induction, H(X_1, ..., X_k) = sum over j of H(X_j | X_1, ..., X_{j-1}) for finitely-valued X_1, ..., X_k. Dividing every term by ln 2 gives the statement in bits.
X and Y take finitely many values
natural logarithms with 0 ln 0 = 0
K_x the conditional pmf where p_X(x) > 0 and any pmf where p_X(x) = 0

rows.title: Hellinger-Toeplitz Theorem
rows.body:
Let H be a Hilbert space and let T: H → H be a linear operator defined on all of H satisfying ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ for all x, y ∈ H. Then T is bounded (hence self-adjoint). More generally, if S, T: H → H are everywhere defined linear operators with ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Sy⟩ for all x, y ∈ H, then both are bounded. Consequently an unbounded symmetric operator can never be defined on the whole space: the domain of an unbounded self-adjoint operator is a proper dense subspace, and specifying that domain is part of specifying the operator.
H is a Hilbert space
T is linear and defined on all of H
T is symmetric on all of H

rows.title: Hellinger distance, normalized so that 0 <= H^2 <= 1
rows.body:
For probability measures P and Q with densities p and q with respect to a sigma-finite measure lambda dominating both, the squared Hellinger distance is H^2(P, Q) = (1/2) integral (sqrt p - sqrt q)^2 d lambda = 1 - integral sqrt(pq) d lambda, where integral sqrt(pq) d lambda is the Hellinger affinity (Bhattacharyya coefficient), and H = sqrt(H^2). The value does not depend on the dominating measure (take lambda = P + Q) and lies in [0, 1]. Some texts omit the factor 1/2, which doubles H^2.
P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space
lambda is sigma-finite and dominates P and Q

rows.title: Kullback-Leibler divergence bounds Hellinger: 2 H^2 <= -2 log(1 - H^2) <= D_KL(P || Q)
rows.body:
P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space with densities p, q with respect to a sigma-finite measure dominating both; d_TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) - Q(A)| = (1/2) integral |p - q| and H^2(P, Q) = (1/2) integral (sqrt p - sqrt q)^2 = 1 - integral sqrt(pq), so 0 <= H^2 <= 1 and H = sqrt(H^2). If P is absolutely continuous with respect to Q and D_KL(P || Q) = integral log(dP/dQ) dP with natural logarithms (possibly +infinity), then 2 H^2(P, Q) <= -2 log(1 - H^2(P, Q)) <= D_KL(P || Q). The second inequality is an equality for P = delta_0, Q = (delta_0 + delta_1)/2, where both sides equal log 2.
P and Q are probability measures
P is absolutely continuous with respect to Q
natural logarithm

rows.title: Hellinger-total variation sandwich: H^2 <= d_TV <= H sqrt(2 - H^2) <= sqrt(2) H, all sharp
rows.body:
P and Q are probability measures on one measurable space with densities p, q with respect to a sigma-finite measure dominating both; d_TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) - Q(A)| = (1/2) integral |p - q| and H^2(P, Q) = (1/2) integral (sqrt p - sqrt q)^2 = 1 - integral sqrt(pq), so 0 <= H^2 <= 1 and H = sqrt(H^2). Then H^2(P, Q) <= d_TV(P, Q) <= H(P, Q) sqrt(2 - H^2(P, Q)) <= sqrt(2) H(P, Q). The bounds are sharp: mutually singular P, Q give H^2 = d_TV = 1, and the pair P_e = (1/2 + e, 1/2 - e), Q_e = (1/2 - e, 1/2 + e) on two points, 0 < e < 1/2, has d_TV = 2e = H sqrt(2 - H^2) exactly, with d_TV / H -> sqrt(2) as e -> 0.

H^2 carries the factor 1/2, so 0 <= H^2 <= 1

rows.title: Shannon Entropy
rows.body: The Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable X with probability mass p is H(X) = - sum over x of p(x) log p(x) (base-2 logarithm for bits), with the convention 0 log 0 = 0. H(X) is nonnegative, at most log of the alphabet size with equality for the uniform distribution, and measures the expected information content or irreducible description length of X.

rows.title: Shannon Source Coding Theorem
rows.body:
Let X_1, X_2, ... be iid copies of a discrete source X with entropy H(X). For every eps > 0 and all large n, blocks of n symbols can be encoded using at most n (H(X) + eps) bits with error probability tending to zero, and conversely any encoding using at most n (H(X) - eps) bits has error probability tending to one. Entropy is thus the exact asymptotic limit of lossless compression per symbol.

rows.title: Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem
rows.body: The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem is a theorem in the field of signal processing which serves as a fundamental bridge between continuous-time signals and discrete-time signals. In the case of uniformly spaced (periodic) sampling, it establishes a sufficient condition on the sample rate that permits a discrete sequence of samples to capture all the information from a continuous-time signal of finite bandwidth, such that the original signal can be reconstructed exactly from those samples.

rows.title: Shannon's source coding theorem
rows.body: In information theory, Shannon's source coding theorem establishes the statistical limits to possible data compression for data whose source is an independent identically-distributed random variable, and the operational meaning of the Shannon entropy.

rows.title: Shannon Entropy
rows.body: For a discrete random variable X taking values in a finite or countable set with probability mass function p(x) = Pr(X=x), the Shannon entropy is H(X) = - sum_{x: p(x)>0} p(x) * log p(x), using the convention 0*log 0 = 0. H(X) is measured in bits when the logarithm has base 2 (or nats for natural log). H(X) >= 0 always, H(X) = 0 exactly when X is deterministic (a single outcome has probability 1), and among distributions on a fixed set of m outcomes, H(X) is maximized, at value log m, by the uniform distribution.

rows.title: Shannon's Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem
rows.body:
For a discrete memoryless channel with finite input alphabet, finite output alphabet, and fixed transition probabilities p(y|x) (the output at each use depends only on the current input, independently of other uses), define the channel capacity C = max_{p(x)} I(X;Y), the maximum over input distributions p(x) of the mutual information between the channel input X and output Y. Then for every rate R < C there exists a sequence of block codes of length n and rate approximately R whose probability of decoding error tends to 0 as n -> infinity. Conversely, for every rate R > C, the probability of decoding error is bounded away from 0 for every sequence of rate-R codes, regardless of how encoding and decoding are chosen.
the channel is discrete and memoryless: each output Y_i depends on the inputs only through a fixed conditional law p(y|x) applied to X_i
block coding is used with block length n tending to infinity
